introduction: “The root of all principles and the cornerstone of all foundations hath ever been, and shall remain, the recognition of God.” The readings say what this knowledge is and is not. It is the purpose of creation and of the gift of understanding; it is not reached by learning or wealth, and the Essence is known to none; it comes through the Manifestation, by the attributes as the sun is known by its rays, to a heart made pure; and good deeds without it are a body without a spirit. The Shema, the Gospel of John, Paul on the wisdom of the world, the Qur’an, Plato’s sun, Pascal’s heart and the Cloud of Unknowing stand near these claims. Others contest them. Mencius finds Heaven by knowing his own nature, and Whitman sees God in every object without wishing to understand; Leigh Hunt’s Abou Ben Adhem loves his fellow men and leads the list; Peter learns that in every nation the one who does right is accepted; Paine calls revelation hearsay, Feuerbach calls God an image of man, and Mill and Darwin stand for the doubts the readings would set aside.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh makes recognition “the whole duty of man”; the Preacher gives that name to fearing God and keeping His commandments. How do the readings relate knowing to doing?

“Behold how ye have allowed your learning to shut you out, as by a veil.” Paul says that knowledge puffs up; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that knowledge is love and urges study. When does learning veil, and when does it open?

The readings hold that God is known only through His Manifestation. Whitman hears and beholds God in every object; Mencius reaches Heaven through his own nature. What would each side say the other is missing?

Good works without the knowledge of God are called a beautiful body without a spirit. Read Abou Ben Adhem, Micah’s three requirements and James’s remark about the devils. What is the “spirit” that the reading says deeds need?

“No man can obtain everlasting life, unless he embraceth … this Revelation.” “In every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted.” How do you read strict and generous sayings side by side, in the Bible, the Qur’an and here?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that religious belief which contradicts science and reason is ignorance, and also turns his hearers from “Darwin’s skepticism”. With Tennyson, Mill and Darwin’s own closing sentence in view, what relation between knowledge of the world and knowledge of God do the readings intend?

outside.why: “The whole duty of man is to recognize Him.” The Preacher’s conclusion uses the same phrase with a different content: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
Recognition is “the root of all principles and the cornerstone of all foundations”. Israel’s foundation is said twice a day: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord.
Once God is recognized, whatever He ordains is binding. John makes the knowing itself the end: this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God.

“Behold how ye have allowed your learning to shut you out, as by a veil.” Paul: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth; if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.

The end of all learning is “the recognition of Him Who is the Object of all knowledge”, and learning has become the veil. Jesus to the learned: ye search the scriptures, and they testify of me, and ye will not come to me.
“First and foremost among these favors … is the gift of understanding.” Aristotle begins from the same gift and its appetite: all men by nature desire to know.

Understanding is given so that the creature may “know and recognize the one true God”, by recognizing His Manifestation. Mencius has a road that runs inward: he who has exhausted his mental constitution knows his nature, and knowing his nature, he knows Heaven. What does each road offer that the other lacks?
“Blessed the ear that hath heard … and the eye that hath seen and recognized the Lord Himself.” Jesus: blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.
People are to “cleanse their hearts from the stain of evil desire … and attain unto the knowledge of the one true God”. The sixth beatitude: blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
“The Ocean of true knowledge hath appeared … Incline your ears.” Isaiah: ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters.
The capacity to know and love God is “the primary purpose underlying the whole of creation”. The Qur’an: I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me.
In the realm of knowledge the lover will “come out of doubt into certitude”. The man born blind, pressed by the learned: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.

Certitude is the lover’s reward for escaping doubt. Tennyson says of a friend who fought his doubts that there lives more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds. Is doubt a place one leaves, or part of the way?
“Whosoever claimeth to know Him is an infidel, by the testimony of his own self.” Laozi: he who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.
The highest knowledge is “to know Him through Him”: “I have known Thee through Thee.” Jesus: neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him.
Man’s highest station is attained “not through learning; inasmuch as in every nation there are learned men”. Paul: where is the wise? where is the scribe? The world by wisdom knew not God.
Nor is it attained through wealth or any transitory thing. Jesus: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
“The Prophets and Messengers of God have been sent down for the sole purpose of guiding mankind.” The Qur’an: there is not a nation but a warner hath passed among them.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes knowledge by conception from knowledge that is intuitive and immediate. Pascal draws a line in the same place for our knowledge of God: it is the heart which experiences God, and not the reason.
“We know not what the reality of the sun is, but we know the sun by the ray, by the heat.” Plato uses the sun for what makes all knowing possible and is itself beyond being known as other things are.
“No one hath any way to the Reality of Deity except through the Instrumentality of the Manifestation.” Jesus: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

There is no way but through the Manifestation, says the reading; to suppose otherwise is “a theory and not a fact”. Whitman supposes otherwise and is at peace: I hear and behold God in every object, yet understand God not in the least. What would the reading say he has, and has not?
“That conception of God which a man has is but a phantasm, an image.” Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, they would make the gods in their own shapes.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that there is “no connection between such a conception and the Supreme Being”. Feuerbach agrees about the conception and denies the Being. What, in these readings, keeps the first statement from becoming the second?
“True knowledge hath ever been, and shall always be, specially reserved unto Him.” The Qur’an: of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little.
“He cannot be known save through Him.” Paul: the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.

“Ignorance is the non-existence of knowledge, and if there were no existence, non-existence could not be.” Augustine argues in the same form about evil: what is it but the absence of good, as disease is the absence of health?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads the alchemist’s sulphur and mercury as the love and the knowledge of God. George Herbert had found the philosopher’s stone in the same quarter: this is the famous stone that turneth all to gold.
“It is only the Divine Light that can give us sight for the invisible things.” The Qur’an’s verse of light: Allah guideth unto His light whom He will.

The intellect understands “all that exists”; another light is needed for what is invisible. Kant, having measured what reason can reach, said that he had to abolish knowledge to make room for belief. Do the reading and Kant put the boundary in the same place?
The great Teachers “became like polished mirrors, reflecting faithfully the Glory of God”. Paul: we all, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image.
Everyone should say: “Thou art the Knower of what is within me, and I know not what is within Thy Self.” These are the words of Jesus in the Qur’an.
“The healer of all thine ills is remembrance of Me, forget it not.” The Qur’an: verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.
“At many a dawn have I turned … unto thine abode, and found thee on the bed of ease busied with others than Myself.” The Apocalypse: behold, I stand at the door, and knock.
“True remembrance is to make mention of the Lord … and forget aught else beside Him.” Jesus to Martha: thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful.
“Open the hidden eye that thou mayest behold the fire of God.” Elisha prays for his servant, and the young man’s eyes are opened on a mountain full of chariots of fire.
“Fear ye God; God will teach you.” Proverbs: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.

In this station knowledge is not sought but given: “Knowledge is a light which God casteth into the heart of whomsoever He willeth.” Jesus names what goes before such knowing: if any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine.
“Unless one recognize God and love Him, his cry shall not be heard.” The Epistle to the Hebrews: he that cometh to God must believe that he is.

The reading makes recognition the condition of being heard. Peter, in a Roman officer’s house, learns something wider than he had thought: in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. How far does the reading’s “recognize” reach?
“Ask thou of God that the magnet of His love should draw unto thee the knowledge of Him.” Jesus: ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find.

The first to believe in Jesus “was a fisherman”, and “the mysteries of wisdom and utterance” flowed from his mouth. The council in Jerusalem saw it: unlearned and ignorant men, and they had been with Jesus.
“Knowledge is love.” The First Epistle of John: he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá joins love with study, listening and thought. The author of the Cloud of Unknowing sets them in order: by love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never.
Without this sight, “even should he possess a hundred thousand eyes, he would still be accounted blind”. Jesus to those sure of their sight: now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
“God willing, may your bewilderment also be in the knowledge of God.” Paul’s is: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!
A bewilderment that is itself a kind of knowing. The psalm: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá divides those who believe in God into those who accept revelation and those who do not. Paine was of the second kind and gave his reason: revelation is revelation to the first person only, and hearsay to every other. What answer do these readings make to him?
“If thou remain heedless of this Most Great Manifestation … to what wilt thou cleave?” Peter, asked whether he too will leave: Lord, to whom shall we go?

“The seeker is missing and the thirsty one deprived, for he knows not the way to the Ocean and has not recognized nor knows the Guide.” An Ethiopian reading Isaiah in his chariot: how can I, except some man should guide me?
“You must endeavor to understand the mysteries of God, attain the ideal knowledge.” Hosea: then shall we know, if we follow on to know the Lord.

“The intellectual proofs of Divinity are based upon observation and evidence.” Paul allows the argument its force: the invisible things of him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá holds that proofs constitute a “decisive argument”. Pascal, as able a reasoner as his century had, thought that by natural light we can know neither what God is nor if He is. What does each man take a proof to be?

Good works without the knowledge of God are “a body of the greatest beauty, but without a spirit”. Leigh Hunt’s poem, learned by generations of schoolchildren, says the opposite: the one who asks only to be written as loving his fellow men leads all the rest. Which do you think truer, and what would change your mind?

The reading asks for knowledge of God besides good deeds. James presses the other side: believing that God is one is no achievement, since the devils also believe, and tremble. If neither deeds alone nor belief alone suffices, what is the knowledge the reading means?

The questioner asks what need the good have of divine teachings. Micah lists what the Lord requires, and it is short: to do justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly with thy God. Does the third item concede the reading’s point?

“The honor of man is through the attainment of the knowledge of God; his happiness is from the love of God.” Augustine: You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless till they rest in You.
“A true philosopher would never deny God nor His evidences.” Bacon: a little philosophy inclineth man’s mind to atheism, but depth in philosophy bringeth men’s minds about to religion.
The knowledge of God “can in no wise be attained save by recognizing Him Who is the Bearer of the Most Great Name”. Jesus to Philip: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Attainment to the Divine Presence is through His presence. Paul at Athens: whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
“Read, in the school of God, the lessons of the spirit, and learn from love’s Teacher.” Jesus: take my yoke upon you, and learn of me.
One must seek heavenly virtues “in order that he may prove to be the image and likeness of God”. The phrase is from the first chapter of Genesis.
“If religious beliefs contradict science and reason, they are assuredly ignorance.” Tennyson hoped for both together: let knowledge grow from more to more, but more of reverence in us dwell.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá makes reason a test of religious belief. Tertullian would not allow the court: what has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What is each afraid of losing?
“I created all things for the knowledge of the Lord of Names. Yet when the veil was lifted … they opposed and turned away.” John: the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.

This is “not the day … to occupy themselves with Voltaire’s doubts or Darwin’s skepticism”. Darwin closed his great book in wonder: there is grandeur in this view of life. Is his science one of the doubts the reading sets aside, or one of the “divine truths” it asks people to pursue?

The reading turns its hearers from doubt to worship. Mill argued that a belief never fully and fearlessly discussed is held as a dead dogma, not a living truth. What place do the readings give to the doubts they name?
“No man can obtain everlasting life, unless he embraceth the truth of this … Revelation.” Peter before the council makes the same kind of claim: there is none other name under heaven given among men.

The reading’s condition is strict. The Qur’an has a verse that names Jews, Christians and Sabaeans and promises that whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does right has nothing to fear. How do exclusive and inclusive sayings live together in one scripture, and in these readings?
The prayer asks for “the sciences that demonstrate the appearance of Thy Beauty in the realm of creation”. The psalm: the heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
“Through insight man attains to faith and wisdom … You see with the inner eye.” Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.

“There are sciences and arts not taught in college, and these are divine knowledge.” The first words revealed to Muḥammad name a teacher beyond the schools: thy Lord, Who teacheth man that which he knew not.
Men give their lives to discover a place on the map, and “no one thinks to discover the Kingdom”. The merchant of the parable does think of it, and sells all that he has.
“Salvation—heaven—is the conscious realisation of God in this life.” Jesus: the kingdom of God is within you.
The learned one who has caught the fragrance of these days “is as the eye for the temple of the world”. The Qur’an: the erudite among His bondmen fear Allah alone.

“The truly learned one is he whose knowledge prevents him from all that My good-pleasure … abhorreth.” The Qur’an asks, of the one who prays at night and the one who does not: are those who know equal with those who know not?

“This is the foundation of the belief of the people of Bahá”, in three sentences. The bishops at Nicaea also set down a foundation in few words. What is a short statement of belief for, and what can it not do?
“If thou hast knowledge of all things but remaineth ignorant of Him of what use … would it be to thee?” Paul: though I understand all mysteries, and all knowledge, and have not charity, I am nothing.

True knowledge of all things follows from knowing Him, says the reading. Pope drew the line the other way for his age: presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man. Which study has the modern world followed, and with what result?
The fruit of earthly existence “is the recognition of the one true God”. Paul: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.
“Thy servant’s shame is to be shut out as by a veil from Thee, and his glory is to know Thee.” Jeremiah: let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.
“Thou Who art my Origin and my Highest Wish … cause me to return.” Boethius: all things yearn in their own way to find their due return.
“Whose nearness is my desire, Whose presence is my dearest wish.” The psalm: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
“Nourish me with the wine of Thy knowledge and the living waters of Thy love.” The psalm: my soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.
“Keep safe Thy servants … from the darts of idle fancy and vain imaginings.” Paul: above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts.
“Thou hast inclined mine ear to Thy voice … and illumined my heart with Thy knowledge.” The disciples at Emmaus, looking back: did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?

The speaker thanks God for having opened his eyes and lit his heart. The Buddha’s last counsel puts the lamp in the disciple’s own hand: be ye lamps unto yourselves; betake yourselves to no external refuge. What does each expect of a person?
“Open the eyes of all that are dear to Thee, that haply they may not be veiled.” An early Christian hymn: awake thou that sleepest, and Christ shall give thee light.

“Whosoever hath recognized Thee will turn to none save Thee, and will seek from Thee naught else except Thyself.” Rābiʿa asks for neither paradise nor safety from the fire, only not to be shut out from the everlasting beauty.
“Thou hast created me, and nourished me … that I may recognize Him Who is the Day-Spring of Thy signs.” The Qur’an: deemed ye then that We had created you for naught?
“Make them to know the Manifestation of Thy Cause.” Paul: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
“Thou art the One through Whom the oceans of knowledge surged.” The Qur’an: though the sea became ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be used up first.

The Báb is “among those who recognize that the knowledge of God … is impossible in its primary essence”. The Vedic hymn of creation ends on the same honesty about the origin of things: he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.

Knowledge of the Essence is impossible, and the Báb says so in a prayer. Wittgenstein’s last proposition would have such things passed over in silence. What is a prayer that begins by confessing it cannot know the One it addresses?
“Remove from sight every veil … until insight penetrates the veils drawn over inner mysteries.” Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
The prayer asks “that all may know Thee as Thou art, though this be greater than all that is great”. The First Epistle of John dares the same hope: we shall see him as he is.
“Verily Thou knowest what profiteth me and what I have, and I know not what Thou hast.” Jesus: your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
“That there may flow from my heart the rivers of Thy knowledge.” Jesus: the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up.
Prayer widens “the circle of divine knowledge”. The one petition for more that the Qur’an puts in its Prophet’s mouth: my Lord! Increase me in knowledge.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá ties growth in knowledge to prayer. Confucius says that he was not born with knowledge but was fond of antiquity and earnest in seeking it there. What are the labours, besides prayer, by which the readings in this guide expect knowledge of God to grow?

jeremiah-glory-in-this.text: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the Lord

hosea-follow-on-to-know.text: Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the Lord: his going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth

jeremiah-search-with-all-your-heart.text: And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart

ecclesiastes-whole-duty-of-man.text: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man

matthew-seek-and-ye-shall-find.text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened

john-do-his-will-shall-know.text: If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself

john-truth-shall-make-you-free.text: If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free

corinthians-knowledge-puffeth-up.text: Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know. But if any man love God, the same is known of him

corinthians-world-by-wisdom.text: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe

john-epistle-loveth-not-knoweth-not.text: Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love

matthew-revealed-unto-babes.text: I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes

james-devils-also-believe.text: Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble

acts-in-every-nation.text: Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him

romans-law-unto-themselves.text: For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts

acts-none-other-name.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved

hebrews-must-believe-that-he-is.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him

quran-whoever-believeth-and-doeth-right.text: Lo! Those who believe (in that which is revealed unto thee, Muhammad), and those who are Jews, and Christians, and Sabaeans - whoever believeth in Allah and the Last Day and doeth right - surely their reward is with their Lord, and there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve.

quran-erudite-fear-allah.text: And of men and beasts and cattle, in like manner, divers hues? The erudite among His bondmen fear Allah alone. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Forgiving.

quran-increase-me-in-knowledge.text: Then exalted be Allah, the True King! And hasten not (O Muhammad) with the Qur'an ere its revelation hath been perfected unto thee, and say: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge.

quran-those-who-know.text: Is he who payeth adoration in the watches of the night, prostrate and standing, bewaring of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord, (to be accounted equal with a disbeliever)? Say (unto them, O Muhammad): Are those who know equal with those who know not? But only men of understanding will pay heed.

quran-read.text: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not

plato-good-as-the-sun.text: You would say, would you not, that the sun is only the author of visibility in all visible things, but of generation and nourishment and growth, though he himself is not generation? Certainly. In like manner the good may be said to be not only the author of knowledge to all things known, but of their being and essence, and yet the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power
plato-good-as-the-sun.author: Plato

pascal-heart-experiences-god.text: It is the heart which experiences God, and not the reason. This, then, is faith: God felt by the heart, not by the reason
pascal-heart-experiences-god.author: Blaise Pascal

whitman-not-curious-about-god.text: And I say to mankind, Be not curious about God, / For I who am curious about each am not curious about God, / (No array of terms can say how much I am at peace about God and about death.) / I hear and behold God in every object, yet understand God not in the least
whitman-not-curious-about-god.author: Walt Whitman

mencius-knows-heaven.text: He who has exhausted all his mental constitution knows his nature. Knowing his nature, he knows Heaven
mencius-knows-heaven.author: Mencius

hunt-abou-ben-adhem.text: "And is mine one?" said Abou. "Nay, not so," / Replied the angel. Abou spoke more low, / But cheerly still; and said, "I pray thee then, / "Write me as one that loves his fellow men." / The angel wrote, and vanish'd. The next night / It came again with a great wakening light, / And show'd the names whom love of God had bless'd, / And lo! Ben Adhem's name led all the rest
hunt-abou-ben-adhem.author: Leigh Hunt

kant-room-for-belief.text: I must, therefore, abolish knowledge, to make room for belief
kant-room-for-belief.author: Immanuel Kant
